content.title: About
content.content: Grits are a coarse ground corn porridge traditionally prepared with water and no added fat. They are available in regular and quick varieties, differing in cooking time.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Grits are a staple in the Southern United States, often served for breakfast with cheese, butter, or seafood.
Quick‑cook grits are ready in 5–7 minutes, while regular grits take about 15–20 minutes.
Corn, the base of grits, has been cultivated for over 7,000 years.
Grits can be yellow or white depending on the corn variety used.
Besides porridge, grits are used in casseroles, soups, and as a side dish.

items.title: Source of complex carbohydrates
items.content: Grits provide slowly digestible energy, helping maintain stable blood‑sugar levels.

items.title: Rich in dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber supports healthy digestion and promotes satiety.

items.title: Contains B‑vitamins
items.content: Grits supply thiamine, niacin, and folate, which are important for energy metabolism.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: When cooked with water only, grits are a low‑calorie option.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: Grits provide iron, magnesium, and phosphorus, essential for blood health and bones.

items.title: Corn allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to corn products.

items.title: High glycemic index
items.content: Grits have a relatively high GI, so people with diabetes should monitor portion sizes.

items.title: Mycotoxin contamination
items.content: Poor‑quality corn can contain mycotoxins; choose reputable brands.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Cook grits in water, seasoning with salt to taste. Serve as a creamy porridge, as a side to meat, fish or vegetables, or incorporate into casseroles and soups.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store grits in an airtight container in a cool, dry place. For long‑term storage, keep them in the refrigerator to prevent mold growth.
